newsitem.title: GERMANY: Snowplows clean up sunny Berlin after Love Parade.
newsitem.headline: Snowplows clean up sunny Berlin after Love Parade.

text.p: Snowploughs took to the sunny streets of Berlin on Sunday to clear up a carpet of cans, bottles and clothing shed during the giant Love Parade techno music fest -- an event which drew up to one million revellers.

The city's sanitation department (BSR) said clean-up crews got off to a late start removing up to 180 tonnes of garbage because massive crowds were still packing the streets hours after Saturday's parade officially ended.

Despite threats by neo-Nazis and anarchist punks before the parade, police said the event ran smoothly with no major disruptions and only 105 people detained, most on charges of selling drugs or picking fights.
"It was a happy, boisterous Love Parade this year and took place without disruption," a police spokeswoman said.
First-aid workers said they treated about 3,000 ravers for exhaustion, dehydration and broken bones but reported no more serious injuries.

Young people from around the world who had descended on Berlin for the weekend partied through the night under the Brandenburg Gate, down the eight-lane parade route and even on the Potsdamer Platz, Europe's largest construction site.

Many police officers seemed to catch "rave fever" too, as they danced along with the thundering bass and synthesizer riffs of techno, had their faces painted with hearts and sunflowers, and playfully exchanged water-gun fire with the overheated crowds.
Police said the event had drawn about 500,000 ravers, but organisers insisted Berlin had hosted about a million street dancers, beating last year's count of 750,000 people.
Those out-of-town guests not still partying on Sunday in more than 130 techno clubs which threw all-night bashes groggily made their way to packed train and bus stations.

Techno music fans and those eager to see the spectacle which has exploded in popularity since its modest beginnings in 1989, shortly before the fall of the Berlin Wall, came from five continents for the city's ninth annual parade.

Hundreds of people who had failed to book accommodation ahead of time camped in the city's Tiergarten park which lines the parade route. Environmentalists said the park looked like a "battlefield", covered with rubbish and exhausted ravers.
Although the BSP provided 672 toilets along the parade route, thousands relieved themselves in the park, a fate environmentalists said was far worse for the soil there than the mountains of garbage.

"We are spraying water above the trees to alleviate the 'over-fertilisation' of the Tiergarten this weekend," said a police officer supervising trucks armed with water cannons which were inching their way down the boulevard.
Parade organisers had tried to initiate an outside "urination ban" to prevent damage to the Tiergarten.
"The crews woke me up this morning at 9.30 a.m.," yawned Steffan, 25, a raver in from Trebbin, south of Berlin. "The hoses came through and drenched us."
Nature lovers had tried to re-route the Love Parade away from the Tiergarten, saying the crush of people would do irreversible damage to the park's fragile ecosystem.

Despite the garbage, disruption and noise, city officials have embraced the Love Parade as a giant money maker for the cash-strapped city. Berlin expects to rake in 150 million marks ($84 million) from the event.

But club owners prove to be the real winners at the festival, luring thousands to continue their dance marathon into the night at a price of up to 50 marks a head, in addition to cashing in on sales from T-shirts, hats and compact discs.

A group of disgruntled disc jockeys, frustrated with what they called the main event's "commercialism" staged a rival "Hate Parade" in eastern Berlin, but police said only about 1,000 attended and it fizzled out after a few hours. ($ = 1.78 German Marks)
